# Stationary and drone-assisted methane plume localization with dispersion spectroscopy

Michael G. Soskind a, Nathan P. Li b, Daniel P. Moore b, Yifeng Chen a,c, Lars P. Wendt b, James McSpiritt b, Mark A. Zondlo b, Gerard Wysocki a,*

a Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA b Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA c Currently at Norsk Elektro Optikk AS, Solheimvegen 62A, 1471 Lørenskog, Norway

A R T I C L E  I N F O

Edited by Menghua Wang

Keywords: Laser spectroscopy Standoff sensing Target tracking Source attribution

A B S T R A C T

This work presents stationary and mobile retroreflector-based remote sensing techniques for methane leak localization and quantification using chirped laser dispersion spectroscopy equipped with a custom laser transceiver capable of continuous tracking of a flying drone and coupled with inverse atmospheric gas dispersion modeling. The techniques demonstrate the ability to localize leaks as low as 0.13 g CH4⋅s−1, which are up to 25 times smaller than those typically observed at natural gas facilities, as well as actively track a moving retrore­ flector mounted on a lightweight (~250 g) drone to enable spatial plume reconstruction. This system exhibited a 2.3 ppm-m sensitivity over pathlengths of 40–150 m. Source localization to within ±7 m is demonstrated using a modified horizontal radial plume mapping technique with a stationary retroreflector grid. Meanwhile, the mobile system utilizing a drone-mounted retroreflector is able to localize a controlled release within ±1 m of its source location and estimate leak rates using inversion techniques assuming type B Gaussian plume stability class within ±30% error with respect to the actual low flow rate releases.

## 1. Introduction

Methane (CH4) is the second most important anthropogenic green­ house gas in the environment and has grown in interest recently due to the growing use of natural gas in residential and commercial settings. Because the primary component of natural gas is CH4, which presents a global warming potential 34 times that of carbon dioxide with carbon feedbacks over a 100-year period (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021), its use as a cleaner fuel requires mitigation and monitoring of fugitive emis­ sions during extraction, processing, and delivery. Furthermore, it was recently shown that even with advanced estimation techniques, there was a discrepancy of 60% between the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) inventory emissions estimates and measurements at nat­ ural gas facilities (Alvarez et al., 2018). These results were compounded by recent results based on satellite data over the Permian Basin, which showed methane fluxes more than two times greater than those of inventory-based measurements (Zhang et al., 2020). Another recent study found that the EPA national emissions estimate may be under­ representing nationwide emissions by approximately 80% (Weller et al.,

2020). Therefore, with nearly a quarter of methane emissions origi­ nating from the energy sector, there is a need for better quantification and characterization of emissions sources from natural gas infrastructure. Conventionally, fugitive emission monitoring and mitigation is implemented with leak detection and repair (also referred to as LDAR) techniques. The most widely accepted techniques are known as Method 21, introduced in 1983 by the EPA as a detection method using portable extractive sensors and optical gas imaging (OGI) cameras, which are handheld instruments that generate images of methane plumes using spectral wavelength filters in front of the imaging sensor (Fox et al., 2019; Ravikumar et al., 2019). These systems require manual operation, leading to missing sporadic ‘superemitter’ events, which contribute to nearly 50% of methane emissions (Zavala-Araiza et al., 2017). While OGI systems are currently widely accepted by regulators and operators in North America, these handheld methods are labor-intensive. Alter­ native screening technologies in addition to Method 21 and OGI exist, including aircraft sensors (Gerilowski et al., 2011), mobile gas labs (Innocenti et al., 2017), satellite-based observations (de Gouw et al.,

2020), and stationary sensors (Alden et al., 2019; Dobler et al., 2017; Michel et al., 2016; Plant et al., 2015). Alternatively proposed, but not yet as widely used as the OGI, are GMAP-REQ and OTM33, which are methods reliant on ground-based vehicles to acquire air pollutant sources located in proximity to the driving route and can allow for source emissions estimates from small releases and up to whole facility measurements (Brantley et al., 2014; Edie et al., 2020). Large leak inventory discrepancies and labor intensity make it essential to develop high-accuracy source-estimation technologies that are efficient and low-cost to capture and resolve large spatial and tem­ poral variability of CH4 emissions. Open-path sensing offers a poten­ tially effective solution for monitoring emissions at local scales (Cossel et al., 2017; Daghestani et al., 2014; Diaz et al., 2016; Golston et al., 2018; Macleod et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2020). Recently, open-path solutions have shown promise in improving sensing of multiple natu­ ral gas distribution facilities, particularly in continuous monitoring ap­ plications (Alden et al., 2019; Coburn et al., 2020). Open-path sensors deployed in high-risk areas can provide continuous readings of methane concentration using a variety of methods. In addition to continuous monitoring at the single or multi-site level as reported in (Cossel et al., 2017; Daghestani et al., 2014; Diaz et al., 2016; Macleod et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2020), it is of interest to further localize fugitive emissions and determine which subsystems of the facility are leaking. This may only be possible with a more agile technique for measuring and moni­ toring at the facility level. In this general area of localization approaches, methods based on unmanned aerial vehicles (also referred to as drones) have started gaining significant attention. Due to their small size and increased mobility, drone-based techniques (Emran et al., 2017; Fox et al., 2019; Gålfalk et al., 2021; Golston et al., 2017, 2018; Iwaszenko et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2012; Marathe, 2019; Nathan et al., 2015; Ravikumar et al., 2019; Tuzson et al., 2020) are of particular interest to bridge the gap between highly localized handheld approaches and large-area satellite and aircraft monitoring techniques. Recent techniques primarily utilize small payload CH4 sensors mounted to the drone body, but this approach faces challenges associated with handling the payloads required with higher precision instruments necessary for leak quantification and localization (Emran et al., 2017; Fox et al., 2019; Golston et al., 2017, 2018; Iwaszenko et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2012; Marathe, 2019; Morales et al., 2022; Nathan et al., 2015; Ravikumar et al., 2019; Tuzson et al., 2020). Therefore, open-path remote sensing systems in combination with reflectors at various fixed locations or with a mobile retroreflector mounted to a drone provide a viable alternative for localizing methane leaks. Potential for implementing such an approach has been discussed briefly in prior research (Cossel et al., 2017) which demonstrated an early open-path sensor with relatively slow (15 Hz) camera-based drone target tracking at kilometer pathlengths to acquire path-integrated spectroscopic signals of atmospheric constituents. To enable full tomo­ graphic reconstruction of chemical plumes and spatial identification of leak locations at facility levels, significantly more agile drone tracking systems are required with bandwidths enabling tracking of the drone motion needed for scanning of 3D space for higher precision emission quantification. In this article, we present the design and experimental demonstration of an open-path remote chirped laser dispersion spectroscopy (CLaDS) sensor enabling two separate methodologies for stationary and droneassisted methane plume reconstruction. The first methodology imple­ ments a stationary multi-reflector system for localizing methane releases using a modified horizontal radial plume mapping technique. The sec­ ond methodology is unique in its implementation, because it allows for active sampling of an open space that was enabled by spatial scanning of a laser beam while tracking a mobile, drone-mounted retroreflector. This methodology is used with inversion techniques to localize and es­ timate the flow rate of simulated methane leaks. The methodologies have been verified in a set of controlled field experiments and show excellent capabilities in terms of leak localization as well as leak rate

estimation.

1.1. CLaDS technique and optical design

CLaDS operates by measuring the dispersion of light in a gas medium using a multi-frequency laser beam. The dispersion information is extracted in real-time by frequency demodulation, with the concentra­ tion determined by spectral fitting to the HITRAN 2016 database for methane (Gordon et al., 2017). During spectral fitting, which occurs during post-processing, there is some offset relative to the LICOR LI- 7810 system that was used for calibration during the measurement, but this offset is accounted for by taking the difference of the acquired concentrations with one another. Additionally, the potential database bias is not expected to have a larger effect on the extracted concentration than the errors in position of the drone or other similar errors assumed in the Gaussian plume fitting or modified horizontal radial plume mapping methods. The spectral region near 1653.7 nm has been chosen, because the methane absorption band exhibits minimal interference with com­ mon atmospheric interferers, including H2O and CO2. Although typi­ cally performed in atmospheric studies, we did not perform a dry concentration correction for CH4, and note that the error of the order of at most 1% that would be expected is much less than that of the Gaussian plume, especially since measurements were performed over <1 h du­ rations. By measuring optical dispersion, CLaDS offers potential ad­ vantages over conventional open-path, absorption-based techniques: namely, the linearity between the measured dispersion and the sample concentration, as well as immunity to intensity or amplitude fluctua­ tions (Wysocki and Weidmann, 2010). Furthermore, the technique al­ lows for real-time optical pathlength measurement, which is crucial in applications with targets varying in distance or location, and allows for an eye-safe, optical fiber based transmitter architecture, enabling robust operation in the field (Hangauer et al., 2021; Plant et al., 2015). The CLaDS technique has been discussed previously in a number of publi­ cations (Chen et al., 2016, 2019, 2021; Hangauer et al., 2021; Plant et al., 2015; Soskind et al., 2019, 2020; Wysocki and Weidmann, 2010), and due to its immunity to intensity noise and linear response to gas concentration, it was selected as the most promising spectroscopic platform to implement reliable plume reconstruction, leak quantifica­ tion, and leak localization using stationary and drone-assisted methodologies.

## 2. Stationary reflector measurements

*Fig. 1 shows a schematic of the CLaDS system that was used in all stationary reflector measurements. Typical open-path chemical sensing systems reported switching times between different reflectors on the order of minutes or left them unreported (Alden et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019, 2021; Dobler et al., 2017; Plant et al., 2015). The work presented here aims at providing retroreflector switching rates on the order of seconds to provide fast spatial scanning and minimize reconstruction errors associated with varying atmospheric (i.e., wind) conditions. This reduction in switching time should enable measurement of shorter timescale events in addition to lower data loss and improved consistency of longer-term emissions measurements. The CLaDS system, schematically shown in Fig. 1, is designed for measurements at distances up to 100 m, which was a good compromise for indoor and early outdoor testing. The design considerations taken into account include transmitter and receiver optics sizes and focal lengths, among other considerations including the steering optic size, and use of a field lens to maintain good signal-to-noise ratio at various distances for the duration of the experiment. The optics is mounted in a 37 × 27 × 14 in. T-slot aluminum cage with electronics in a 12 U 19 in. rack. It weighs approximately 150 lbs., and can be loaded into a van with 2 people. A fiber-coupled laser diode (NTT Electronics, NLK1U5FAAA, LD1) targeting the R3 methane line near 1653.7 nm is passed through an isolator after a chirp modulation with 10 kHz triangular waveform from*

an external arbitrary function generator (Tektronix AFG3102) is applied via laser drive current modulation. The laser is temperature stabilized to 28.9 ± 0.02 ◦C using a thermoelectric cooler and controller (Thorlabs TED200). This spectral region is well separated from potential common spectral interferers within the chirp span of 0.9 cm−1. After the isolator, 10% of the light is directed into a wavelength- and chirp-calibration arm that performs direct absorption spectroscopy using a fiber-coupled reference methane gas cell (GC 1, Wavelength Reference, 20% methane) and a fast photodetector (FPD1, Thorlabs DET01CFC). 90% of the light is directed into the sensing path, and it passes through an electro-optic modulator (EOM, Thorlabs LN81S) creating 1 GHz modu­ lation sidebands for CLaDS detection. Those modulation sidebands are additionally modulated with a 340.33 MHz⋅s−1 chirp used for simulta­ neous distance measurement (Hangauer et al., 2021). After the EOM, another 90/10 splitter is placed in the path, with 10% of light being directed to a second gas cell (GC 2, Wavelength Reference 1% methane) and fast photodetector (FPD 2, Menlo Systems FPD310) used as a con­ centration reference for the free-space sensing channel. These compo­ nents comprise the core CLaDS instrument. The light in the sensing path is then combined with light from a fiber coupled red laser (LD2) and sent through a reflective collimator (COL, Thorlabs RC08APC-P01). The collimated beam is launched via a series of turning mirrors (M1, M2) and a motorized gimbal mirror (GM, Newmark Systems GM-6) towards multiple broadband hollow retroreflectors (RRX, Newport BBR2.5-2I). The light reflected from the retroreflectors is then collected by a Newtonian telescope (modified Celestron 127EQ), represented by a primary mirror (PM) and secondary mirror (M3), with a negative field lens (FL, Thorlabs LC4252-C) used to re-collimate the collected laser beam. The collected light is separated by a dichroic beamsplitter into a visible camera channel (CAM, Thorlabs DCC1240C equipped with 100 mm fixed focal length objective lens, OL, Thorlabs MVL100M23) and an infrared signal channel containing a fast photo­ detector (FPD 3, Menlo FPD310-F) with 25 mm focal length collection lens (L1, Thorlabs LA1951-C). The same CLaDS core instrument is used for both stationary and drone-assisted methane plume detection meth­ odologies, although the drone-assisted system required development of dedicated optical hardware and control electronics to accomplish fast and precise tracking of a drone-based reflector. The system configuration incorporates several layers of autoalignment hardware and software to decrease the switching time when compared to the systems reported in the literature. An important component of the pointing and tracking mechanism is the motorized gimbal itself. The motorized gimbal demonstrated a repeatability of approximately 0.02◦. Offsets of 0.02◦cause errors when switching be­ tween multiple targets, due to the portion of light returning from the

retroreflector not being focused effectively on the small diameter (40 μm) fast photodetector. Therefore, the gimbal mirror position is opti­ mized after each motion to increase the return optical power on the detector and improve the signal to noise after FM demodulation of the signal due to the system backlash. The error signal between the current position and desired position is derived from a visible-light camera paired with a short-pass dichroic mirror which reimages the scene within the telescope’s entire field of view. The camera is co-aligned to the return path and images the scene similarly to the collection optics for the fast spectroscopic detector in the infrared signal channel. In addition to imaging used for coarse scene alignment, the camera is co-aligned with a visible laser beam to provide a direct error signal for control­ ling the angle of the motorized gimbal mirror. This is implemented via a centroid-based image processing technique described in Supplementary Material section S.1, which is used to control the gimbal relative angle via a software-based proportional-integral (PI) feedback loop. As a result, this centroid based active alignment system can provide retro­ reflector switching times on the order of seconds as shown in the time series of collected path-normalized concentrations and pathlengths shown in Fig. 2a. In the figure, the system performed switching and realignment in an average of 5 s between each retroreflector, enabling collection of spectroscopic data during the experiment with high effec­ tive duty cycle. The entire experiment took nine minutes to complete acquisition of signals from all 16 reflectors each averaged for ~25 s. During these measurements, the acquired signal was >1 μW approxi­ mately 80% of the time, a threshold that assures at least 10 ppm-m sensitivity of the system. This power requirement was also used to filter out data with poor signal to noise ratio. Lower return powers could be used, but would require additional averaging time, or alternatively switching to heterodyne enhanced chirped laser dispersion spectroscopy (Chen et al., 2021).

2.1. Source localization via modified horizontal radial plume mapping

The traditional Horizontal Radial Plume Mapping (HRPM) technique was developed for use with open-path, path-integrated optical remote sensing systems, and designed to locate sources of fugitive emissions close to the ground. Adopted by the EPA, the originally published method sampled a 3 × 3 grid of pixels, and the sensing instrument was placed at one of the corners of the grid (Hashmonay et al., 2008). Several modifications to this original arrangement were implemented in this work. The number of reflectors was expanded to a 4 × 4 grid, and we altered the location of the sensing instrument. A slight increase in the number of retroreflectors allows for additional points to help localize the plume within the sampled grid. The 4 × 4 grid was a reasonable

2.2. Stationary reflector - field experiment configuration

We performed one set of controlled methane releases near the West Windsor Fields (40.33901 N, 74.64031 W) on the campus of Princeton University. Fig. 2c shows the experimental setup for one measurement during the release. A 4 × 4 grid of retroreflectors was set up such that the wind direction should nominally be parallel to one of the grid axes, and the grid was set up a day prior to the release experiments based upon the forecast wind direction. The grid position selection and marking took a few hours the day prior to measurement, while the retroreflector placement was performed on the day of the experiments by placing the retroreflectors mounted to tripods on the pre-marked positions in a large field. This design is typical of horizontal radial plume mapping tech­ niques, but not strictly necessary in order to accurately localize the plume. The wind direction during the experiment happened to be different than the forecast and was not parallel to the grid axes, and although not optimal for plume reconstruction, still successfully pro­ vided approximate localization of the plume. The impact of non-optimal wind direction and speeds primarily affects the number of downwind reflectors that can see a concentration difference. If the wind is not parallel to the grid, fewer retroreflector measurements contribute to the plume reconstruction. However, it should be noted that the wind

Fig. 2c indicates the fit concentration of the plume for each grid cell using the modified HRPM technique. Windy conditions, particularly wind gusts >10 m⋅s−1 can affect the laser beam alignment by inducing motion of the system installed on a cargo van as well as via the mechanical stability of retroreflectors mounted on economy camera tripods. During windy conditions in the field, these effects were clearly noticeable as an increased measurement noise within the CLaDS spectra. The early version of the instrument relied on active beam pointing methodology with limited tracking bandwidths due to slow camera frame rates and lag induced by buffer overflow and were insufficient to mitigate the rapid misalignments due to signal instabilities caused by wind gusts but allowed for slow opti­ mization of return signal during calm conditions. Since the phase demodulation at low return powers requires signal averaging over 1 s intervals, any laser beam pointing deviation during the measurement causes an increased phase noise averaged into the final measurement. Despite those early limitations, we were able to demonstrate that the CLaDS system can operate in the field in temperatures as cold as −6 ◦C and with wind gusts >10 m⋅s−1. The mobile-reflector tracking capabil­ ities developed for later experiments are discussed in the following sections and have also largely mitigated the negative effects of wind gusts in a stationary retroreflector setup, improving the measurement quality and robustness in stationary configurations.

## 3. Mobile reflector measurements

In many applications, installation of additional sensing

infrastructure is not feasible. For instance, setting up a series of re­ flectors may be challenging along pipelines or at natural gas facilities. However, if measurements could be taken with a drone-based retrore­ flector, the infrastructure and the setup requirements become minimal. (Marathe, 2019), for example, proposes drones for methane sensing in conditions that may be dangerous for humans to operate. Furthermore, this could reduce the time needed for performing surveys, and generate potential cost savings.

3.1. Optical system for mobile reflector tracking

Although the stationary reflector setup discussed in the previous section can maintain strong return signals from retroreflectors using a centroid detection algorithm implemented with a visible camera, the low tracking bandwidth cannot be used to actively track a rapidly moving mobile retroreflector or respond to wind gusts affecting the position stability of the instrument vehicle and retroreflector. In addi­ tion to the requirement of increasing tracking bandwidth, there is a noticeable lag in the camera-based tracking system due to the camera missing frames and filling up the buffer while in operation. It may benefit future experiments to use a specialized frame grabber with highspeed camera and real-time software if an image processing-based error calculation is to be performed, as the lag led to significant tracking de­ lays and resulted in loss of tracking for instances of relatively modest acceleration. To address the increased bandwidth needs for tracking rapidly moving reflectors, the system’s target tracking system was completely redesigned to enable tracking of drone-mounted reflectors using an inline quadrant photodetector, as shown in Fig. 3. The same CLaDS fiber-based transmitter design as in the stationary setup is also used in the mobile tracking configuration. The launch beam is collimated (COL, Thorlabs F810APC-1550) and co-aligned to a 3 in. off-axis parabola (Thorlabs custom OAP), as shown in Fig. 3 (but there is no co-propagating visible beam used in this setup). The launch beam is directed towards the retroreflector (RR, Newport 50,326–1010) moun­ ted to a drone (DJI Mavic Mini) using a motorized gimbal mirror (GM, Aerotech AMG-150) that is different than that used in the previously discussed stationary system. The Newtonian telescope design used in the stationary system was replaced with an off-axis parabolic telescope design to provide better collection performance for the retroreflecting target at shorter distances. The new telescope design uses a shorter focal length primary telescope mirror (150 mm as compared to the previous 450 mm), which results in a shorter depth of field, smaller focal spot (due to a faster reflective surface) and requires less accommodation of the system at different positions of the retroreflector in the Z-dimension. This allows for the system to passively maintain relatively constant power at different distances from the transceiver, while having no need for an additional optic for adjustment in Z, as was previously required for the stationary retroreflector configuration (FL in Fig. 1). This design change is discussed in Supplementary Material section S.4. The light reflected by the retroreflector is collected by the primary off-axis parabola, which forms a reflective telescope with a secondary off-axis parabola introducing a 3:1 reduction in beam size. Part of the received beam is then coupled to a fast-photodetector (FPD3) to extract the spectroscopic signal, while a second part of the beam is analyzed by a quadrant photodetector (Thorlabs PDQ30, QPD) used to track the drone. Initial tests of the system used a visible laser and a visible quadrant photodiode, but after testing in sunny conditions, we switched to an InGaAs quadrant detector and the CLaDS near-infrared laser source, which assured significantly less interference from background solar ra­ diation, but reduced the amount of return light in the CLaDS arm by 3 dB. Fortunately, we could account for this loss in our power budget. The light collected by FPD3 is demodulated using a custom FPGA program to extract the dispersion signal in real time with 1 Hz refresh rate (Chen et al., 2016). Since tracking is primarily performed using the infrared QPD channel, the additional visible imaging channel has been separated from the infrared channel by placing the visible CMOS camera (CAM in

To address the need for tracking of a fast-moving retroreflector target, we developed an active control technique using the infrared light emitted by the measurement laser and a quadrant photodetector in a focal plane of the receiver optics for fast error signal generation. This more advanced approach has been enabled by the new servo-based Aerotech gimbal, which offers analog inputs equipped with an inter­ nal, embedded PII2 control that allows implementation of fast feedback control. By using the error signal coming from the quadrant photode­ tector (QPD in Fig. 3), we were able to extract the relative beam align­ ment error with respect to the center of the quadrant detector. This returns a feedback signal in both the x and y directions that is fed back into the control unit. By using this feedback, we applied an error correction signal to track the moving target. Additional electronics were developed to bias the detector, extract the data from the quadrant de­ tector, and transfer those signals to the Aerotech gimbal controllers via analog input ports. The signals can be transferred at kHz rates, and the error signal is subsequently read by the on-board analog-digital con­ verter at kHz rates by the Aerotech controllers, enabling up to 40 Hz electronic control signal bandwidths, with no lag in the system caused by transferring data from a buffer. The error signal was aligned to have its zero crossing at the optimal signal return location, and a model was constructed and verified with experimental data, described in more detail in Supplementary Material section S.5. An additional media file, Visualization 1, shows a video of the drone tracking capabilities during field tests of the system, with an inset graph showing the return optical power and methane path-integrated concentration during flight.

3.2. Mobile retroreflector - field experiment configuration

The system was deployed in the same open field near Princeton University as the stationary configuration to measure the methane plume distribution from a controlled CH4 release. The release rate of methane during the experiments was 23.5 ± 0.5 L⋅min−1 (0.26 g CH4⋅s−1 0.86 SCFM). This represents a release rate approximately 12 times lower than those caused by natural gas facilities leaks (Sub­ ramanian et al., 2015). The mean wind speed on the test day was 3.5 m⋅s−1, and the experiments were performed at a release height of approximately 1.5 m, with the drone flown at approximately 1.5 m. Fig. 5 shows the approximate GPS locations of the weather tower, in­ strument van, methane release point, and reference LI-COR CH4 trace gas analyzer (LI-7810). The position error of a mobile phone GPS unit used in this measurement is represented by the light-colored ring sur­ rounding the mean GPS positions for all static equipment locations (excluding drone positions). The mean GPS locations of the Mavic Mini drone, based on measurements taken with the onboard GPS sensor, are shown as colored circles. The color represents the mean methane con­ centrations measured for the duration of the drone hovering over the region. Two experiments were performed, with 30 s and 60 s hover durations. There was not a significant difference between the results obtained with these two durations, which is as expected for type B Gaussian plume stability class (Fritz et al., 2005). In contrast to our stationary measurements, which required a few hours to set up, these two 6 × 6 grid flight acquisitions were performed over 45 min and 60 min durations and took 4–6 drone flights each without the need for preset infrastructure. It is worth noting that with longer drone flight times now available with commercial drones having improved battery per­ formance, we expect a further reduction of the measurement time that can potentially be performed during a single flight, which is highly promising for real-world sensing scenarios. The comparison of the anticipated (open circles) and measured (colored circles) positions are overlaid on top of one another. The discrepancy between the anticipated and measured locations are well within the expected positioning error of manual flights.

3.3. Inversion technique

The general method for localizing the leak, and estimation of the release rate is shown schematically in Fig. 6. The method begins with an approximate location of both the CLaDS instrument as well as drone locations, both based on GPS coordinates. In these tests the GPS co­ ordinates are used to fit the data, although the optical system was used to confirm the distances estimated by the GPS positions (in the future the distance measurement capability of CLaDS coupled with calibrated gimbal azimuth and elevation data could be used for full 3D plume approximation, but the absolute gimbal position calibration has not been available with the current system). The three-dimensional Gaussian plume model (Seinfeld and Pandis, 2016) has been used to approximate the path integrated concentrations to the drone locations based on the wind speed and direction. The Gaussian plume model has been implemented previously for plume estimation in a number of ex­ periments for methane sensing (Caulton et al., 2018; Fritz et al., 2005). The Gaussian plume model assumes a near ground point source emitting at a constant rate and offers a representative model for time-integrated data. Alternative techniques have been proposed for similar applica­ tions, such as bootstrap inversion (Alden et al., 2018) and backward Lagrangian stochastic techniques (Gao et al., 2008), but we find that the Gaussian plume model provides a good approximation for the steady controlled release of methane, with each flight lasting <10 min. This is despite the fact that the given model is designed to represent a timeaveraged plume over 20–70 min. The measurement/averaging time is important to consider, and although not studied extensively in this article, previous studies have been performed to optimize the mea­ surements for flux retrieval with different stability classes (Fritz et al., 2005). The 3-D Gaussian plume model is discussed in more detail in Supplementary Material section S.6. We use the Gaussian plume model in conjunction with a rotation of axes, in order to model path integrated concentration measurements using the open-path CLaDS system. This is done by a numerical line integral approximation for each of the open-path measurements with 0.1 m resolution. The analysis could perform gridding to more measurement locations, or even use the exact drone locations during measurement, but the predetermined 6 × 6 grid provides sufficient resolution for an initial characterization of this method with sufficiently fast computation of the estimated source location. The larger arrays with the alternative methods prove slightly more computationally expensive, but may provide more precise locali­ zation for future experiments. The final steps are to localize the plume by finding the global mini­ mum mean square error, as represented in Fig. 6c and Fig. 6d. The inset to the figure is visualized as the maximum of the inverse mean square error, iMSE, defined below:

iMSE = MSE−1 = n ∑n i=1(̂x −x)2 (1)

where ̂x represents the modeled data for the fit, and x represents the data collected by the system, and n is the number of measurements performed. The process of finding the minimum mean square error first requires identifying a likely source location region. During this identification step, we assume a height of the release close to the actual height of the release point. This is an important assumption, and we expect that this would not be needed had we performed a vertical scan of the release slightly downwind to extract the approximate release height. This can be done by performing a vertical radial plume collection with the drone as well. The likely source region is selected as the eastern half of the sampled area, particularly close to the edge of the sampled area, as this is where the concentrations were highest during measurement and the region is shown in Fig. 6c. A coarse search across this area is performed

in 1 m increments to find an approximate leak location in a computation efficient manner, at 4 different flow rates in approximately 15 min. Next, after a maximum was found within the region of interest using the coarse technique, the system searched a smaller region within 1 m of the initial maximum, as shown in Fig. 6d in approximately another 15 min. At this stage, 10 different flow rates were tested, to maximize the inverse mean square error as described in Eq. (1). Finally, Fig. 6e shows the model plume that most closely matches the data collected during the flights. There is no interpolation in space in the least fit process, nor in the emission rate, and instead we pick fixed points to test. However, we do interpolate the image of the gaussian plume for visual purposes. This method for sequential search takes approximately half an hour to average the data and search through the controlled release space considered. This computation time can be further reduced with more effective convex optimization methods, but that was not considered in this work and will be the topic of future system developments.

## 4. Conclusions and future outlook

Finding better techniques for localizing and quantifying methane leaks is an important goal for the natural gas industry to preserve their natural gas product during transport and improve economic outcomes while simultaneously reducing negative environmental impacts. The article describes potential benefits of using two alternative open-path sensing system configurations to localize and estimate the flux from an unknown source of methane. The CLaDS technique, which holds many advantages over other open-path techniques, was used to show­ case recent methane localization and flux estimation experiments with a field-tested spectroscopic system. The system first performed measure­ ments with a stationary configuration of reflectors, with which a controlled methane leak was localized to an approximate grid cell location. The system was then modified to enable active tracking of a rapidly moving retroreflector. This system was used with a drone-based retroreflector and showed promise by performing measurements with minimal infrastructure and was able to localize the leak location to within 1-m during two separate experiments. Furthermore, the system could estimate the release rate within ±30% error with respect to the actual low-flow rate releases, which is comparable to other studies that quantify leak rates (Alden et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2008). Using drones, however, does pose some challenges, such as consistency and precision

of altitude measurements, along with low wind speeds and high direc­ tional variability for mass balance or Gaussian plume estimates (Caulton et al., 2014; Morales et al., 2022). The effect of such uncertainties on open path measurements will be interesting to study in the future with larger sets of measurements. The implementation of a drone gives the second technique tremendous flexibility in selecting the measurement grid via optimized flight patterns, which can potentially translate to an increased plume interception probability and on-demand adjustments of the spatial resolution of the plume retrieval. In the future we plan to optimize the drone flight path to increase measurement coverage while optimizing data collection for accurately performing emissions estimates using the described inversion tech­ niques, or alternative techniques such as computed tomography (Byer and Shepp, 1979). For instance, more accurate emissions height esti­ mates could be performed by incorporating additional height data from the drone flights. Moreover, a drone-based system provides added flexibility to be extended to three-dimensional plume reconstruction methodologies for improved localization and leak rate estimations, and can be easily adopted to measurements of other trace gases for a variety of applications including security, air quality monitoring, or hazardous materials detection. Additional system improvements such as an increased target tracking bandwidth, optimized system beam launching architecture, faster steering optics, and increase of sensing distance by increasing the output optical power are also being considered (Bauer et al., 2015), with more powerful lasers potentially enabling remote sensing and spaceborne applications. Moreover, performing measure­ ments in a controlled release setting at facilities set up for blind release experiments would be a natural next step to assess the capabilities of the developed sensing technologies. ***
